claimant_lives_in_uk.description: Whether the claimant lives in the UK.

children.description: A list of children the claimant is claiming for.

lives_with_claimant.description: Whether the child lives with the claimant.

in_approved_education.description: Whether the child is in approved education or training (e.g. A-levels, GCSEs, NVQ up to level 3). Only relevant for children aged 16-19.

in_extension_period.description: Whether the child (aged 16 or 17) has left education and registered with a government-sponsored careers service or the armed forces (qualifying for a 20-week extension).

upkeep_per_week.description: The amount in £ per week the claimant contributes towards the child's upkeep (food, clothes, pocket money, etc.). Only relevant if the child does not live with the claimant.

another_claimant_has_priority.description: Whether another person who also lives with the child has priority for claiming Child Benefit.

another_claimant_lives_with_child.description: Whether someone who lives with the child is already claiming Child Benefit for them.

care_weeks.description: The number of weeks the child has been in local authority care.

care_home_24h_per_week.description: Whether the child spends at least 24 hours per week at home while in local authority care.

hospital_weeks.description: The number of weeks the child has been in hospital or residential accommodation.

claimant_spends_on_child.description: Whether the claimant regularly spends money on the child (e.g. food, clothes, books) while the child is in hospital or residential accommodation.

is_fostered.description: Whether the child is fostered by the claimant.

council_pays_for_child.description: Whether the local council pays towards the child's accommodation or maintenance.

works_24_plus_hours.description: Whether the child works 24 or more hours per week in paid employment.

started_apprenticeship_in_england.description: Whether the child has started an apprenticeship in England.

receives_qualifying_benefits.description: Whether the child receives qualifying benefits in their own right, such as Universal Credit or Employment and Support Allowance.

conversation.text:
I'd be happy to help you determine if you're eligible for Child Benefit. To assess your eligibility, I'll need to ask you some questions about your situation.

Let me start with the basics:

**Do you have any children, and if so, how many children are you asking about?**

conversation.author: actor
conversation.text: Yes, I have one child I'm asking about - my son Alex, he's 11 years old.

conversation.author: eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Thank you for that information. So you have one child, Alex, who is 11 years old.

Now I need to ask you a few more questions to assess your eligibility:

**Do you live in the UK?**

conversation.author: actor
conversation.text: Yes, I live in the UK.

conversation.author: eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Great, thank you. Now I need to understand your relationship with Alex:

**Do you live with Alex, or if not, do you contribute at least the same amount as Child Benefit towards his upkeep (for example on food, clothes, or pocket money)?**

conversation.author: actor
conversation.text: Yes, Alex lives at home with me.

conversation.author: eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Perfect. Just a few more questions to complete the assessment:

**Is anyone else currently claiming Child Benefit for Alex?**

conversation.author: actor
conversation.text: No, nobody else is claiming Child Benefit for him.

conversation.author: eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Thank you. One final question:

**Is Alex currently in hospital, residential care, or living with someone else for an extended period?**

conversation.author: actor
conversation.text: Actually, yes - Alex has been in hospital for a few months now.

conversation.author: eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
I see. This is an important detail that affects Child Benefit eligibility. I need to understand more about this situation:

**How many weeks has Alex been in hospital so far?**

conversation.author: actor
conversation.text: He's been in hospital for 15 weeks.

conversation.author: eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Thank you for that information. This is important because there are specific rules about Child Benefit when a child is in hospital for more than 12 weeks.

**Do you regularly spend money on Alex while he's in hospital (for example, on clothes, personal items, treats, or other things for him)?**

conversation.author: actor
conversation.text: I'm not sure, to be honest. I mean, I want to help him, but I'm not certain whether what I've been doing counts as regularly spending money on him.

conversation.author: eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
I understand - it can be unclear what counts. Let me ask it differently to help clarify:

**Have you been buying things for Alex during his hospital stay - such as clothes, toiletries, books, toys, treats, or other personal items? And if so, roughly how often have you been doing this?**

conversation.author: actor
conversation.text: Well, I have been getting him some things here and there, but I'm really not sure if it's been regular enough or if it counts. It's hard to say exactly how often.

conversation.text:
## My Assessment

Based on the information you've provided, **I cannot make a definitive determination about your eligibility for Child Benefit for Alex**.

Here's why:

**What works in your favor:**
- You live in the UK
- Alex is 11 years old (under 16)
- You live with Alex (when he's not in hospital)
- No one else is claiming Child Benefit for him

**The complicating factor:**
Alex has been in hospital for 15 weeks, which is longer than the 12-week limit. Normally, after 12 weeks in hospital, you would no longer be entitled to Child Benefit. **However**, there is an important exception: you can continue to receive Child Benefit if you **regularly spend money on your child** while they're in hospital.

**Why it's indeterminate:**
You've indicated that you have been buying some things for Alex "here and there," but you're uncertain whether this counts as "regularly spending money" on him. Without clear information about the frequency and consistency of your spending, I cannot definitively determine whether you meet this exception.

**What I recommend:**
You should contact HMRC's Child Benefit Office directly to discuss your specific situation. They can review the details of what you've been spending on Alex and help determine whether this meets the requirement for continuing Child Benefit payments. They're best placed to make this assessment based on the full details of your circumstances.
